messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rohan, a twenty-year-old writer with a quiet intensity, traces his current state of paralysis back to a Tuesday afternoon six months ago. He was at a workshop, deeply engrossed in editing a short story, when he realized he was late to pick up his younger sister, Priya. He remembers the flicker of annoyance, the quick text message telling her to get a ride with her friend Sarah. He remembers the relief of not having to rush. That relief is now the memory that haunts him most, because an hour later, his phone rang with his mother’s frantic voice. There had been an accident. By the time he reached the hospital, Priya was gone. The world, as he knew it, ended in the sterile quiet of a waiting room, under the hum of fluorescent lights.

In the months that followed, the initial shock curdled into a set of rigid, terrifying beliefs. Rohan became convinced that the world was not just indifferent, but actively malevolent and unpredictable. His prior assumptions about fairness and safety felt like a cruel joke; his beliefs about how life was supposed to work had been utterly shattered. This pervasive sense of a dangerous world meant he could never truly be at ease. Even in his own apartment, a space once dedicated to creative focus, he remains in a constant state of high alert, unable to relax. He spends his nights staring at the ceiling, his mind racing, and the slightest noise from the street—a car door slamming, a distant siren—causes him to jolt upright, his heart hammering against his ribs as if expecting another catastrophic phone call.

This profound conviction that disaster is always imminent has reshaped his life. He has come to believe that any happiness is fleeting and that making plans is simply an invitation for fate to intervene. As a result, he systematically avoids committing to anything in the future. Invitations from friends to concerts or weekend trips are met with vague excuses. The idea of buying a ticket for an event weeks away feels reckless, like tempting the same cruel randomness that took his sister. To manage the unceasing anxiety, he calls his parents multiple times a day, the conversations circling the same desperate script: "Are you okay? Is everything alright?" He is seeking reassurance not just for their safety, but for his own precarious sense of stability, needing someone else to confirm, just for a moment, that the world is holding together.

His avoidance, meant to protect him, has instead become a cage, reinforcing his darkest conclusions about himself and the world. By turning down every social invitation and refusing to plan beyond the next twenty-four hours, his world has shrunk to the four walls of his apartment. This self-imposed isolation serves as daily proof for his belief that he is no longer the happy, engaged person he once was, but someone fundamentally broken and miserable. Each time he dodges a reminder of Priya—changing the radio station when her favorite song comes on, taking a long detour to avoid their old park—he confirms to himself that the grief is too big, that he is too weak to handle it, and that the only sane response to a hostile world is to hide from it.

These very strategies, designed to reduce his distress, perversely keep his nervous system on a knife's edge. The constant vigilance required to avoid grief triggers means a part of his mind is always scanning his environment for potential threats, leaving him perpetually tense and exhausted. Because he never allows himself to experience a planned event that goes well or to sit with a memory of his sister without falling apart, he never gets any evidence to contradict his fear. His mind and body remain primed for a catastrophe that has already happened, trapped in the immediate aftermath. This state of constant, low-grade panic has made sleep a near impossibility, further fraying his ability to cope during the day.

Rohan sought therapy after his agent, concerned by months of silence, sent an email asking if he was alright. He has stared at the unopened message for a week, the notification a symbol of a professional and creative life that is slipping through his fingers. He confessed that he hasn’t written a single new word since the accident. He is terrified that engaging with the world again will only lead to more pain, but he is even more terrified of this empty, silent life becoming permanent. He wants, more than anything, to believe in the future again, but he no longer remembers how.
